exercises.title: Truth table with three statements
exercises.description: Create the truth table for $(A \land B) \rightarrow C$. For which assignments is the statement false?
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
With three statements there are $2^3 = 8$ assignments. We first compute the part $A \land B$ and then evaluate the implication.

Step 2: Recall the implication
$P \rightarrow Q$ is false only if $P$ is true and $Q$ is false; otherwise it is true.

Step 3: Truth table
$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c} A & B & C & A \land B & (A \land B) \rightarrow C \\ \hline T & T & T & T & T \\ T & T & F & T & F \\ T & F & T & F & T \\ T & F & F & F & T \\ F & T & T & F & T \\ F & T & F & F & T \\ F & F & T & F & T \\ F & F & F & F & T \end{array}$

Step 4: Reading off
The statement is false only for $A = T$, $B = T$, $C = F$ (second row). In all other $7$ cases it is true.

Step 5: Takeaway: What to remember
An implication is false when the hypothesis is true and the conclusion false. Equivalently: $(A \land B) \rightarrow C \equiv A \rightarrow (B \rightarrow C)$ (currying).

exercises.title: Negation of an implication
exercises.description: Determine the negation of “If it rains, the street gets wet.” and show with a truth table that $\neg(A \rightarrow B) \equiv A \land \neg B$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
An implication $A \rightarrow B$ is refuted by a case in which $A$ holds but $B$ does not. This is exactly what $A \land \neg B$ expresses.

Step 2: Truth table
$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} A & B & \neg(A \rightarrow B) & A \land \neg B \\ \hline T & T & F & F \\ T & F & T & T \\ F & T & F & F \\ F & F & F & F \end{array}$

Step 3: Comparison
The last two columns agree in all rows, so $\neg(A \rightarrow B) \equiv A \land \neg B$.

Step 4: Application to the sentence
Negation: “It rains **and** the street does not get wet.” — not “If it rains, the street does not get wet.” (that is not a negation because for $A = F$ both statements are true).

Step 5: Takeaway: What to remember
Common mistake: writing the negation of an implication as an implication again. Rule of thumb: “counterexample = hypothesis true, claim false”.

exercises.title: Necessary and sufficient
exercises.description: Let $A$: “$n$ is divisible by $6$” and $B$: “$n$ is even” (for $n \in \mathbb{N}$). Does $A \Rightarrow B$ hold? Does $B \Rightarrow A$ hold? Phrase this with “necessary” and “sufficient”.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
We check both directions: one direction we justify in general, for the other we look for a counterexample.

Step 2: $A \Rightarrow B$
If $n = 6k$ then $n = 2\cdot(3k)$ is even. The implication holds.

Step 3: $B \Rightarrow A$
Counterexample: $n = 4$ is even but not divisible by $6$. The converse does not hold.

Step 4: Wording
$A$ is **sufficient** for $B$ (anyone divisible by $6$ is even), and $B$ is **necessary** for $A$ (anyone not even cannot be divisible by $6$). $A$ is not necessary for $B$, $B$ is not sufficient for $A$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What to remember
For $A \Rightarrow B$ the hypothesis is sufficient, the conclusion necessary. A single counterexample refutes a universal statement, but many examples do not prove it.

exercises.title: Tautology, contradiction, satisfiable
exercises.description: Classify as tautology, contradiction or satisfiable (but not a tautology): (a) $(A \rightarrow B) \lor (B \rightarrow A)$, (b) $A \land \neg A$, (c) $A \rightarrow \neg A$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
A statement is a **tautology** if it is true under every assignment, a **contradiction** if it is never true, and **satisfiable** if it is true under at least one assignment.

Step 2: (a)
If $A = F$ then $A \rightarrow B$ is true; if $A = T$ then $B \rightarrow A$ is true. In every case one part is true, so the disjunction is always true: **tautology**.

Step 3: (b)
$A$ and $\neg A$ are never true simultaneously: **contradiction**.

Step 4: (c)
For $A = T$, $A \rightarrow \neg A$ equals $T \rightarrow F = F$. For $A = F$ it is $F \rightarrow T = T$. So true for $A = F$, false for $A = T$: **satisfiable but not a tautology** (it is equivalent to $\neg A$).

Step 5: Takeaway: What to remember
$\varphi$ is a tautology exactly when $\neg\varphi$ is a contradiction. The class can also be determined without a full table by case distinction.

exercises.title: Quantifiers and their order
exercises.description: Decide which statements over $\mathbb{R}$ are true: (a) $\forall x\, \exists y: x + y = 0$, (b) $\exists y\, \forall x: x + y = 0$, (c) $\forall x\, \exists y: y^2 = x$, (d) $\exists x\, \forall y: x \leq y^2$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
The order of quantifiers is crucial: in $\forall x\, \exists y$ the $y$ may depend on $x$, in $\exists y\, \forall x$ a single $y$ must work for all $x$.

Step 2: (a) true
For each $x$ choose $y = -x$. Then $x + y = 0$.

Step 3: (b) false
A fixed $y$ would have to satisfy $x + y = 0$ for all $x$. For $x = -y$ it holds, for $x = -y + 1$ it does not. So false.

Step 4: (c) false
For $x = -1$ there is no real $y$ with $y^2 = -1$. So false (over $\mathbb{R}$; over $\mathbb{C}$ it would be true).

Step 5: (d) true
Choose $x = 0$. Then $0 \leq y^2$ for all $y \in \mathbb{R}$.

Step 6: Takeaway: What to remember
From $\exists y\, \forall x\, P$ it follows that $\forall x\, \exists y\, P$, but not conversely ((a) and (b) show this). To refute a universal statement a counterexample suffices, to prove an existence statement an example suffices.

exercises.title: Truth Tables for Logical Operators
exercises.description: Construct the truth table for the operators $\land$ (AND), $\lor$ (OR), and $\rightarrow$ (implication) for the propositions $A$ and $B$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: List all possible assignments for $A$ and $B$:

\begin{array}{c|c}
A & B \\\hline
T & T \\
T & F \\
F & T \\
F & F \\
\end{array}

Step 2: Truth table for $A \land B$ (AND):

\begin{array}{c|c|c}
A & B & A \land B \\\hline
T & T & T \\
T & F & F \\
F & T & F \\
F & F & F \\
\end{array}

Step 3: Truth table for $A \lor B$ (OR):

\begin{array}{c|c|c}
A & B & A \lor B \\\hline
T & T & T \\
T & F & T \\
F & T & T \\
F & F & F \\
\end{array}

Step 4: Truth table for $A \rightarrow B$ (implication):

\begin{array}{c|c|c}
A & B & A \rightarrow B \\\hline
T & T & T \\
T & F & F \\
F & T & T \\
F & F & T \\
\end{array}

exercises.title: Verifying Logical Equivalence with Truth Tables
exercises.description: Verify whether the propositions $A \rightarrow B$ and $\neg A \lor B$ are logically equivalent by constructing a truth table.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Construct the truth table:

\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c}
A & B & \neg A & A \rightarrow B & \neg A \lor B \\\hline
T & T & F & T & T \\
T & F & F & F & F \\
F & T & T & T & T \\
F & F & T & T & T \\
\end{array}

Step 2: Compare columns:
The columns for $A \rightarrow B$ and $\neg A \lor B$ are identical.

Step 3: Conclusion:
The propositions $A \rightarrow B$ and $\neg A \lor B$ are logically equivalent.

exercises.description: Show that the propositions $A \rightarrow B$ and $\neg B \rightarrow \neg A$ are logically equivalent.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Construct the truth table:

\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c}
A & B & \neg A & \neg B & A \rightarrow B & \neg B \rightarrow \neg A \\\hline
T & T & F & F & T & T \\
T & F & F & T & F & F \\
F & T & T & F & T & T \\
F & F & T & T & T & T \\
\end{array}

Step 2: Compare columns:
The columns for $A \rightarrow B$ and $\neg B \rightarrow \neg A$ are identical.

Step 3: Conclusion:
The propositions are logically equivalent.

exercises.title: Exclusive OR
exercises.description: Show that the exclusive OR $A \oplus B$ is equivalent to $(A \lor B) \land \neg (A \land B)$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Construct the truth table:

\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c}
A & B & A \oplus B & A \lor B & A \land B & \neg (A \land B) & (A \lor B) \land \neg (A \land B) \\\hline
T & T & F & T & T & F & F \\
T & F & T & T & F & T & T \\
F & T & T & T & F & T & T \\
F & F & F & F & F & T & F \\
\end{array}

Step 2: Compare columns:
The columns for $A \oplus B$ and $(A \lor B) \land \neg (A \land B)$ are identical.

Step 3: Conclusion:
The equivalence is proven.

exercises.title: Biconditional
exercises.description: Show that the biconditional $A \leftrightarrow B$ is equivalent to $(A \rightarrow B) \land (B \rightarrow A)$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Construct the truth table:

\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c}
A & B & A \leftrightarrow B & A \rightarrow B & B \rightarrow A & (A \rightarrow B) \land (B \rightarrow A) \\\hline
T & T & T & T & T & T \\
T & F & F & F & T & F \\
F & T & F & T & F & F \\
F & F & T & T & T & T \\
\end{array}

Step 2: Compare columns:
The columns for $A \leftrightarrow B$ and $(A \rightarrow B) \land (B \rightarrow A)$ are identical.

Step 3: Conclusion:
The equivalence is proven.

exercises.title: Determining normal forms
exercises.description: Determine a disjunctive normal form (DNF) and a conjunctive normal form (CNF) for $A \rightarrow (B \land C)$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
A DNF is a disjunction of conjunctions (OR of ANDs), a CNF a conjunction of disjunctions (AND of ORs). First we rewrite the implication: $A \rightarrow X \equiv \neg A \lor X$.

Step 2: DNF
$A \rightarrow (B \land C) \equiv \neg A \lor (B \land C)$. This already is a DNF (clauses $\neg A$ and $B \land C$).

Step 3: CNF via distributive law
$
eg A \lor (B \land C) \equiv (
eg A \lor B) \land (
eg A \lor C)$. This is a CNF with two clauses.

Step 4: Check with an assignment
For $A = T$, $B = T$, $C = F$: original $T \rightarrow (T \land F) = T \rightarrow F = F$. CNF: $(F \lor T) \land (F \lor F) = T \land F = F$ ✓. DNF: $F \lor (T \land F) = F$ ✓.

Step 5: Takeaway: What to remember
Every statement has a DNF and a CNF (e.g. from the true or false rows of the truth table). The second distributive law $X \lor (Y \land Z) \equiv (X \lor Y) \land (X \lor Z)$ is the way from DNF to CNF.

exercises.title: Simplifying with laws of logic
exercises.description:
Simplify (a) $(A \lor B) \land (A \lor 
eg B)$ and (b) $(A \land B) \lor (A \land 
eg B) \lor (
eg A \land B)$ using laws of logic.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
We apply distributivity, complement laws ($X \lor \neg X \equiv T$, $X \land \neg X \equiv F$) and identity laws ($X \land T \equiv X$, $X \lor F \equiv X$).

Step 2: (a) Transform
Factoring out $A$ (distributive law backwards): $(A \lor B) \land (A \lor \neg B) \equiv A \lor (B \land \neg B) \equiv A \lor F \equiv A$.

Step 3: (b) First two clauses
$(A \land B) \lor (A \land \neg B) \equiv A \land (B \lor \neg B) \equiv A \land T \equiv A$.

Step 4: (b) Third clause
So the expression is $\equiv A \lor (\neg A \land B)$. Distributive law: $\equiv (A \lor \neg A) \land (A \lor B) \equiv T \land (A \lor B) \equiv A \lor B$.

Step 5: Check with truth values
(b): For $A = F$, $B = T$ the original expression is true (third clause) and $A \lor B = T$ ✓; for $A = B = F$ all clauses are false and $A \lor B = F$ ✓.

Step 6: Takeaway: What to remember
The trick “factor out, then use $X \lor \neg X$ or $X \land \neg X$” simplifies many expressions. A truth table always serves as an independent check.

exercises.title: Negating continuity
exercises.description: Continuity of $f$ at $a$ reads $\forall \varepsilon > 0\ \exists \delta > 0\ \forall x: (|x - a| < \delta \rightarrow |f(x) - f(a)| < \varepsilon)$. Form the negation and use it to show that the step function $f(x) = 1$ for $x \geq 0$, $f(x) = -1$ for $x < 0$ is not continuous at $a = 0$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
When negating, swap every quantifier ($\forall \leftrightarrow \exists$) from the outside in and finally negate the statement. The negation of an implication is $P \land \neg Q$.

Step 2: Negate step by step
$
eg orall\varepsilon\,\exists\delta\, orall x\,(P ightarrow Q) \equiv \exists\varepsilon\, orall\delta\,\exists x\,
eg(P ightarrow Q) \equiv \exists\varepsilon\, orall\delta\,\exists x\,(P \land 
eg Q)$.

Step 3: Negation in words
“There is an $\varepsilon > 0$ such that for every $\delta > 0$ there is an $x$ with $|x - a| < \delta$ and $|f(x) - f(a)| \geq \varepsilon$.”

Step 4: Application to the step function
Choose $\varepsilon = 1$. Let $\delta > 0$ be arbitrary. Choose $x = -\frac{\delta}{2}$. Then $|x - 0| = \frac\delta2 < \delta$, but $|f(x) - f(0)| = |-1 - 1| = 2 \geq 1$.

Step 5: Conclusion
The negation of continuity holds, so $f$ is not continuous at $0$.

Step 6: Takeaway: What to remember
Every refutation in analysis depends on negating quantifier chains (discontinuity, divergence, …). The order of $\varepsilon$ (first) and $\delta$ (afterwards, may depend on $\varepsilon$) is preserved in dual form.

exercises.title: Direct proof by cases
exercises.description: Prove: for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $n^2 + n$ is even.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
We give a direct proof. Since every natural number is even or odd, a case distinction with two cases suffices.

Step 2: Case 1: $n$ even
Let $n = 2k$. Then $n^2 + n = 4k^2 + 2k = 2(2k^2 + k)$. This is divisible by $2$.

Step 3: Case 2: $n$ odd
Let $n = 2k + 1$. Then $n^2 + n = (4k^2 + 4k + 1) + (2k + 1) = 4k^2 + 6k + 2 = 2(2k^2 + 3k + 1)$. This is even as well.

Step 4: Alternative argument
$n^2 + n = n(n+1)$ is a product of two consecutive numbers. One of them is even, so the product is even.

Step 5: Takeaway: What to remember
Case distinctions must be **exhaustive** (here: even/odd). Even numbers are written $2k$, odd numbers $2k+1$. A proof is complete only when all cases are treated.

exercises.title: Valid and invalid arguments
exercises.description: Check whether the following arguments are valid: (a) $A \rightarrow B,\ \neg B \ \therefore\ \neg A$ (modus tollens), (b) $A \rightarrow B,\ B \ \therefore\ A$. Justify with an assignment or truth table.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
An argument is **valid** if in every assignment in which all premises are true the conclusion is true as well. A single counterexample (premises true, conclusion false) makes it invalid.

Step 2: (a) Modus tollens
Let $A ightarrow B$ and $
eg B$ be true. If $A$ were true then $A ightarrow B$ would force $B$ to be true, contradicting $
eg B$. So $A$ is false, i.e. $
eg A$ is true: **valid**.

Step 3: (b) Affirming the consequent
Choose $A = F$, $B = T$. Then $A \rightarrow B$ is true ($F \rightarrow T$), $B$ is true, but the conclusion $A$ is false. Counterexample: **invalid** (the fallacy “affirming the consequent”).

Step 4: Everyday example
(a) “If it rains the street is wet. The street is not wet. So it is not raining.” ✓ (b) “If it rains the street is wet. The street is wet. So it is raining.” ✗ (the street could also be wet because of a burst pipe).

Step 5: Takeaway: What to remember
Valid: modus ponens ($A, A \rightarrow B \therefore B$) and modus tollens. Typical fallacies: affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent ($A \rightarrow B, \neg A \therefore \neg B$).

exercises.title: Determining Normal Forms: CNF and DNF
exercises.description: Determine the conjunctive normal form (CNF) and disjunctive normal form (DNF) of the proposition $\neg (A \rightarrow B)$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Rewrite the implication:
$A ightarrow B \equiv 
eg A \lor B$.
Thus, $
eg (A ightarrow B) \equiv 
eg (
eg A \lor B)$.

Step 2: Apply De Morgan's Law:
$
eg (
eg A \lor B) \equiv A \land 
eg B$.

Step 3: DNF:
$A \land \neg B$ is already in disjunctive normal form, as it is a single conjunction (a term).

Step 4: CNF:
$A \land \neg B$ is also in conjunctive normal form, as it is a conjunction of literals ($A$ and $\neg B$).

Step 5: Verification via truth table:

\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
A & B & A \rightarrow B & \neg (A \rightarrow B) \\\hline
T & T & T & F \\
T & F & F & T \\
F & T & T & F \\
F & F & T & F \\
\end{array}
For $A \land \neg B$:

\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
A & B & \neg B & A \land \neg B \\\hline
T & T & F & F \\
T & F & T & T \\
F & T & F & F \\
F & F & T & F \\
\end{array}
The truth values match, confirming $A \land \neg B$ is both DNF and CNF.

exercises.title: Quantifiers and Their Negation
exercises.description: Formulate the negation of the statement: $\forall x \in \mathbb{N}: \exists y \in \mathbb{N}: x < y$ and write the negated statement in the simplest form.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Original statement:
'For every natural number $x$, there exists a natural number $y$ such that $x < y$.'

Step 2: Apply negation rules:
$\neg (\forall x \exists y: x < y) \equiv \exists x \forall y: \neg (x < y) \equiv \exists x \forall y: x \geq y$.

Step 3: Simplify the negated statement:
'There exists a natural number $x$ such that for all natural numbers $y$, $x \geq y$.' This implies $x$ is the largest natural number.

Step 4: Contextual verification:
In $\mathbb{N}$, there is no largest number, so the negated statement is false, which aligns with the original statement being true.

Step 5: Final form:
The negation is: 'There exists a natural number $x$ that is greater than or equal to every natural number $y$.'

exercises.title: Logical Inference
exercises.description: Show that from the premises $A \rightarrow B$ and $B \rightarrow C$, the conclusion $A \rightarrow C$ logically follows.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Construct the truth table:

\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c}
A & B & C & A \rightarrow B & B \rightarrow C & A \rightarrow C \\\hline
T & T & T & T & T & T \\
T & T & F & T & F & F \\
T & F & T & F & T & T \\
T & F & F & F & T & F \\
F & T & T & T & T & T \\
F & T & F & T & F & T \\
F & F & T & T & T & T \\
F & F & F & T & T & T \\
\end{array}

Step 2: Analyze the truth table:
In rows where both premises ($A \rightarrow B$ and $B \rightarrow C$) are true (rows 1, 5, 7, 8), the conclusion $A \rightarrow C$ is also true.

Step 3: Conclusion:
The logical inference is valid.

exercises.title: Quantifiers and Their Negation
exercises.description: Formulate the negation of the statement: $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}: \exists y \in \mathbb{R}: x^2 + y^2 = 1$ and simplify it.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Original statement:
'For every real number $x$, there exists a real number $y$ such that $x^2 + y^2 = 1$.'

Step 2: Apply negation rules:
$\neg (\forall x \exists y: x^2 + y^2 = 1) \equiv \exists x \forall y: x^2 + y^2 \neq 1$.

Step 3: Simplify the negated statement:
'There exists a real number $x$ such that for all real numbers $y$, $x^2 + y^2 \neq 1$.'

Step 4: Verification:
The original statement is true (for any $x$, $y = \sqrt{1 - x^2}$ exists for $|x| \leq 1$, and adjust accordingly). The negation is false, as no such $x$ exists, confirming logical consistency.

Step 5: Final form:
The negation is: 'There exists a real number $x$ such that $x^2 + y^2 \neq 1$ for all real numbers $y$.'

exercises.title: Logical Inference with Quantifiers
exercises.description: Show that from $\forall x: P(x) \rightarrow Q(x)$ and $\exists x: P(x)$, the conclusion $\exists x: Q(x)$ logically follows.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Analyze the premises:
1. $\forall x: P(x) \rightarrow Q(x)$: For all $x$, if $P(x)$, then $Q(x)$.
2. $\exists x: P(x)$: There exists an $x$ such that $P(x)$.

Step 2: Logical inference:
Let $a$ be an element such that $P(a)$ (from premise 2).
From premise 1, $P(a) \rightarrow Q(a)$ holds.
Since $P(a)$ is true, $Q(a)$ follows by modus ponens.
Thus, there exists an $x$ such that $Q(x)$.

Step 3: Formal proof:
- Premise 2: $\exists x: P(x)$, so there is some $a$ with $P(a)$.
- Premise 1: $\forall x: P(x) \rightarrow Q(x)$, so $P(a) \rightarrow Q(a)$.
- Since $P(a)$, we have $Q(a)$.
- Therefore, $\exists x: Q(x)$.

Step 4: Conclusion:
The inference is valid.

exercises.title: Logical Equivalence with Quantifiers
exercises.description: Show that $\forall x: (P(x) \land Q(x))$ and $(\forall x: P(x)) \land (\forall x: Q(x))$ are logically equivalent.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Analyze the first statement:
$\forall x: (P(x) \land Q(x))$ means: For all $x$, both $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ hold.

Step 2: Analyze the second statement:
$(\forall x: P(x)) \land (\forall x: Q(x))$ means: For all $x$, $P(x)$ holds, and for all $x$, $Q(x)$ holds.

Step 3: Prove equivalence:
- Forward: If $\forall x: (P(x) \land Q(x))$, then for all $x$, $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$. Thus, $\forall x: P(x)$ and $\forall x: Q(x)$, so $(\forall x: P(x)) \land (\forall x: Q(x))$.
- Backward: If $\forall x: P(x)$ and $\forall x: Q(x)$, then for each $x$, $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$, so $\forall x: (P(x) \land Q(x))$.

Step 4: Conclusion:
The statements are logically equivalent.

exercises.title: Logical Equivalence with Existential Quantifier
exercises.description: Show that $\exists x: (P(x) \lor Q(x))$ and $(\exists x: P(x)) \lor (\exists x: Q(x))$ are logically equivalent.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Analyze the first statement:
$\exists x: (P(x) \lor Q(x))$ means: There exists an $x$ such that $P(x)$ or $Q(x)$ holds.

Step 2: Analyze the second statement:
$(\exists x: P(x)) \lor (\exists x: Q(x))$ means: There exists an $x$ such that $P(x)$, or there exists an $x$ such that $Q(x)$.

Step 3: Prove equivalence:
- Forward: If $\exists x: (P(x) \lor Q(x))$, then there is some $x$ where $P(x)$ or $Q(x)$. Thus, either $\exists x: P(x)$ or $\exists x: Q(x)$, so $(\exists x: P(x)) \lor (\exists x: Q(x))$.
- Backward: If $\exists x: P(x)$ or $\exists x: Q(x)$, then there is some $x$ with $P(x)$ or some $x$ with $Q(x)$, implying $\exists x: (P(x) \lor Q(x))$.

Step 4: Conclusion:
The statements are logically equivalent.

exercises.title: Irrationality of √2
exercises.description: Prove by contradiction that $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
In a proof by contradiction one assumes the opposite of the claim and derives a contradiction. Here: assume $\sqrt2 \in \mathbb{Q}$, written as a fully reduced fraction.

Step 2: Assumption
Suppose $\sqrt2 = \frac pq$ with $p,q \in \mathbb{N}$ and $\gcd(p,q) = 1$.

Step 3: Square
$2 = \frac{p^2}{q^2}$, so $p^2 = 2q^2$. Hence $p^2$ is even.

Step 4: Lemma: $p^2$ even $\Rightarrow$ $p$ even
Contrapositive: if $p$ is odd, $p = 2k+1$, then $p^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1$ is odd. Hence: $p^2$ even $\Rightarrow$ $p$ even.

Step 5: Contradiction
By the lemma $p = 2m$. Substituting: $4m^2 = 2q^2$, so $q^2 = 2m^2$ and thus $q$ is even too. Then $2$ divides both $p$ and $q$, contradicting $\gcd(p,q) = 1$.

Step 6: Conclusion
The assumption is false, so $\sqrt2$ is irrational. $\blacksquare$

Step 7: Takeaway: What to remember
A proof by contradiction shows $\neg A \Rightarrow F$, hence $A$. The reduced fraction is the trick that makes the contradiction possible.

exercises.title: Infinitely many primes
exercises.description: Prove Euclid's theorem: there are infinitely many primes.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
We show: for every finite list of primes there is another prime not on the list. For this we need that every number $> 1$ has a prime divisor.

Step 2: Assumption
Suppose there were only finitely many primes $p_1, p_2, \dots, p_n$.

Step 3: Construction
Consider $N = p_1 p_2 \cdots p_n + 1$. We have $N > 1$, so $N$ has a prime divisor $q$ (e.g. the smallest divisor $> 1$).

Step 4: $q$ is not on the list
If $q = p_i$ for some $i$, then $q$ would divide the product $p_1 \cdots p_n$ and $N$, hence also the difference $N - p_1 \cdots p_n = 1$. Impossible.

Step 5: Contradiction
So $q$ is a prime not among $p_1,\dots,p_n$ — contradicting the assumption that the list contains all primes. $\blacksquare$

Step 6: Takeaway: What to remember
Important: $N$ itself need not be prime (e.g. $2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13 + 1 = 30031 = 59 \cdot 509$); only its prime divisor is new. A classic proof by contradiction.

exercises.title: Injectivity formally: quantifiers and negation
exercises.description: Write “$f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is injective” with quantifiers, form the negation and use it to refute the injectivity of $f(x) = x^2$. Prove the injectivity of $g(x) = 3x - 5$ from the definition.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
We formalise the definition, negate it systematically and apply both to concrete functions: refuting by counterexample, proving by calculation.

Step 2: Definition
$f$ injective $\iff \forall x\, \forall y: (f(x) = f(y) \rightarrow x = y)$.

Step 3: Negation
$
eg orall x\, orall y\,(P ightarrow Q) \equiv \exists x\,\exists y\,(P \land 
eg Q)$, so: $f$ not injective $\iff \exists x\, \exists y: (f(x) = f(y) \land x 
eq y)$.

Step 4: Refutation for $x^2$
Choose $x = 2$, $y = -2$. Then $f(x) = 4 = f(y)$ but $x \neq y$. The negation holds, so $f$ is not injective.

Step 5: Proof for $3x - 5$
Let $x,y \in \mathbb{R}$ be arbitrary with $g(x) = g(y)$, i.e. $3x - 5 = 3y - 5$. Add $5$ and divide by $3$: $x = y$. So the definition holds for all $x,y$: $g$ is injective.

Step 6: Takeaway: What to remember
Proof (universal statement): pick arbitrary elements and derive the claim. Refutation (existential statement of the negation): give **one** concrete counterexample.

exercises.title: The empty set and vacuous truth
exercises.description: Determine the truth values: (a) $\forall x \in \emptyset: x > 5$, (b) $\exists x \in \emptyset: x > 5$, (c) “Every prime between $24$ and $28$ is even.” (d) $\emptyset \subseteq A$ for every set $A$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Universal statements about empty sets are **vacuously true**: there is no counterexample. Existential statements about empty sets are false: there is no example.

Step 2: (a) true
$\forall x \in \emptyset: P(x)$ means “for all $x$: $x \in \emptyset \rightarrow P(x)$”. The hypothesis $x \in \emptyset$ is always false, so the implication is always true.

Step 3: (b) false
$\exists x \in \emptyset: P(x)$ demands an $x$ with $x \in \emptyset \land P(x)$. There is no $x \in \emptyset$, so the statement is false.

Step 4: (c) true
Between $24$ and $28$ lie $25,26,27$; none of them is prime. The set of such primes is empty, so the universal statement is (vacuously) true.

Step 5: (d) true
$\emptyset \subseteq A$ means $\forall x\,(x \in \emptyset \rightarrow x \in A)$, again vacuously true. The empty set is a subset of every set.

Step 6: Takeaway: What to remember
The truth value “$F \rightarrow Q$ is true” is the reason. The principle explains why $\emptyset \subseteq A$ and $\sum_{k \in \emptyset} a_k = 0$ are sensible conventions. One says: “All unicorns are pink” is true.

exercises.title: Proof by Contraposition and Contradiction
exercises.description: Prove by contraposition and by contradiction: 'If $n^2$ is even, then $n$ is even.'
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Proof by contraposition:
The contrapositive is: 'If $n$ is odd, then $n^2$ is odd.'
Let $n = 2k + 1$ (odd).
Then $n^2 = (2k + 1)^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1$, which is odd.
Thus, the contrapositive holds, proving the original statement.

Step 2: Proof by contradiction:
Assume $n^2$ is even and $n$ is odd.
If $n$ is odd, $n = 2k + 1$, so $n^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1$, which is odd.
This contradicts the assumption that $n^2$ is even.
Thus, $n$ must be even.

Step 3: Conclusion:
Both proof methods confirm that if $n^2$ is even, then $n$ is even.

exercises.title: Logical Equivalence with Nested Quantifiers
exercises.description: Show that $\forall x \exists y: P(x,y)$ and $\neg \exists x \forall y: \neg P(x,y)$ are logically equivalent.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Analyze the first statement:
$\forall x \exists y: P(x,y)$ means: For every $x$, there exists a $y$ such that $P(x,y)$.

Step 2: Analyze the second statement:
$
eg \exists x  orall y: 
eg P(x,y) \equiv  orall x \exists y: P(x,y)$, since:
$
eg (\exists x  orall y: 
eg P(x,y)) \equiv  orall x 
eg ( orall y: 
eg P(x,y)) \equiv  orall x \exists y: P(x,y)$.

Step 3: Prove equivalence:
The logical transformation shows both statements are identical.
- First statement: Every $x$ has some $y$ with $P(x,y)$.
- Second statement: It is not the case that there exists an $x$ such that for all $y$, $P(x,y)$ is false, which means for every $x$, there is some $y$ with $P(x,y)$.

Step 4: Conclusion:
The statements are logically equivalent.

exercises.title: Logical Equivalence with Complex Quantifier Combinations
exercises.description: Show that $\forall x: (P(x) \rightarrow \exists y: Q(x,y))$ and $\forall x \exists y: (P(x) \rightarrow Q(x,y))$ are logically equivalent.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Analyze the first statement:
$\forall x: (P(x) \rightarrow \exists y: Q(x,y))$ means: For all $x$, if $P(x)$, then there exists a $y$ such that $Q(x,y)$.

Step 2: Analyze the second statement:
$\forall x \exists y: (P(x) \rightarrow Q(x,y))$ means: For all $x$, there exists a $y$ such that if $P(x)$, then $Q(x,y)$.

Step 3: Prove equivalence:
- Forward: If $\forall x: (P(x) \rightarrow \exists y: Q(x,y))$, then for each $x$, if $P(x)$, there is some $y$ with $Q(x,y)$. Thus, for each $x$, there exists a $y$ such that $P(x) \rightarrow Q(x,y)$ holds.
- Backward: If $\forall x \exists y: (P(x) \rightarrow Q(x,y))$, then for each $x$, there is a $y$ such that $P(x) \rightarrow Q(x,y)$. If $P(x)$, then $Q(x,y)$ for some $y$, so $\exists y: Q(x,y)$, hence $P(x) \rightarrow \exists y: Q(x,y)$.

Step 4: Conclusion:
The statements are logically equivalent.

solutionSteps:
Step 1: Analyze the first statement:
$\neg \forall x: (P(x) \rightarrow Q(x))$ means: It is not the case that for all $x$, if $P(x)$, then $Q(x)$.

Step 2: Rewrite using quantifier negation:
$

Since $P(x) ightarrow Q(x) \equiv

Thus, $\exists x: (P(x) \land

Step 3: Analyze the second statement:

exercises.title: Logical Equivalence with Nested Quantifiers and Implications
exercises.description: Show that $\forall x: (P(x) \rightarrow \forall y: (Q(y) \rightarrow R(x,y)))$ and $\forall x \forall y: ((P(x) \land Q(y)) \rightarrow R(x,y))$ are logically equivalent.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Analyze the first statement:
$\forall x: (P(x) \rightarrow \forall y: (Q(y) \rightarrow R(x,y)))$ means: For all $x$, if $P(x)$, then for all $y$, if $Q(y)$, then $R(x,y)$.

Step 2: Analyze the second statement:
$\forall x \forall y: ((P(x) \land Q(y)) \rightarrow R(x,y))$ means: For all $x,y$, if $P(x)$ and $Q(y)$, then $R(x,y)$.

Step 3: Prove equivalence:
- Forward: Assume the first statement. For any $x,y$, if $P(x) \land Q(y)$, then from $P(x)$, we have $\forall y: (Q(y) \rightarrow R(x,y))$, so $Q(y) \rightarrow R(x,y)$. Since $Q(y)$, $R(x,y)$ follows.
- Backward: Assume the second statement. For any $x$, if $P(x)$, then for any $y$, if $Q(y)$, then $P(x) \land Q(y)$, so $R(x,y)$ by the second statement. Thus, $\forall y: (Q(y) \rightarrow R(x,y))$.

Step 4: Conclusion:
The statements are logically equivalent.
